text: cap-land's PR-create retry loop falls back to 'gh pr view $CAP_BRANCH' which matches a PR by branch name regardless of state (open/closed/merged). After a branch name is reused (e.g. cap-restack pushes a rebased branch with the same name after its old PR was closed), this makes cap-land print a stale 'PR: <old-closed-url>' and exit as if it succeeded, when no new PR was actually opened. Hit this twice landing caefisica/drive#2 and #3 equivalents after restacking. Fix: the gh pr view fallback should filter --state open, or verify the returned PR's headRefOid matches the just-pushed commit before trusting it. Still open after the 2026-09-10 cap-land rewrite (directory-pinning, 8-attempt backoff): the view fallback is unchanged.

text: `pgrep -f` is unusable for polling task processes once `cap send` has revived a session, because the revive puts the captain's entire message inside the launch prompt and the harness carries that prompt in its argv. A gate round's instructions run to several thousand characters and quote the exact commands the agent is told to run, so `pgrep -f 'mise run check'` matched the claude session itself, not the check. Hit twice in a row today on local-env: two `until ! pgrep -f ...; do sleep; done` waiters never terminated because the agent's own command line kept matching, and one had to be killed by hand. Anything that waits on a task's real work should watch the work's own output file or pid, or at least anchor the pattern to the binary (`pgrep -f '^mise '`, `pgrep -x`), never a phrase that could appear in a brief or a captain message. Worth considering whether cap-send should pass the revival text through a file or stdin instead of argv, since argv is world-readable on this box and the same message can carry findings that quote source.

text: killing cap-gate does not kill the review it launched, so the account keeps paying for an Opus session whose verdict nobody will ever record. herdr starts the reviewer in its own pane, detached from cap-gate's process tree, so when the harness's low-memory guard killed the backgrounded `cap gate local-env --full` seconds after it started, the wrapper died and the opus process (pid 1637014, pane w2:p1E) carried on reviewing for another ten minutes with nothing left to read its output, promote the report or call gate_record. Recovered by hand this time: waited on the orphan's pid, read the pane, wrote notes/classroom/local-env.gate-A.md and called gate_record with the fingerprint directly. The same shape applies to any interruption of cap-gate, Ctrl-C included, and it is worse than a wasted review because state/tasks/<slug>/gate.json still holds the previous round's verdict at a stale fingerprint, which reads exactly like a gate that was never run. cap-gate should either trap EXIT and close the pane it opened, or record enough (pane id, fingerprint, profile) that a later run can adopt an orphaned review instead of paying for it twice. Followed up 2026-09-10, fourteen hours later: pid 1637014 was still resident and idle, holding 211MB, long after its task record had been dropped and its findings had been recovered by hand into notes/classroom/defects.md. Killing it returned about 900MB. So the cost is not only the wasted review, it is a process that never exits and that nothing in Captain knows about, on a box whose low-memory guard then starts killing live work instead: it reaped three of the captain's own background waiters while the orphan it could not see kept its memory. Whatever cap-gate records about a review it launches has to include the pid, so a later run can reap it as well as adopt it.

text: A reviewer that cannot run the thing it reviews reports its own uncertainty as a defect, and the report gives the captain no way to tell that apart from a real finding. Gate B on cap-headless raised two findings in round two, both worded as risks the captain should verify before landing: /compact may not work in headless print mode, and usage_write may read wrong rate-limit field paths. Both are wrong, and one live claude -p --resume "/compact" plus one live rate_limit_event settled them in under a minute. Round one B had already invented a deleted paper-cut entry from a stale base. The same profile passed local-env in the same period after running the config generator in an isolated fake repo, reading Moodle core to confirm exit-code branching, and checking that the pinned Docker tags exist, so this is not a weak model. It is a reviewer placed where it could not execute, saying so, and having that read as a verdict. Gate A in the same rounds reproduced three of its four findings against a stubbed harness. Two fixes worth weighing: give the review profile whatever it needs to exercise the code, and make the report separate a reproduced defect from a suspicion so the captain sees which is which without reading every paragraph. The second is plan Stage 3.

text: cap gate paid for two full reviews of an empty diff, and would have printed READY TO LAND for a task with nothing to land. Its guard counts commits (`git rev-list --count $CAP_BASE..HEAD`), which stays above zero for a branch whose content is already in the base, either because sync_base merged the base back in or because the work landed by another route. local-env hit both: its dev stack went onto classroom master as ea3ecec2..41477d00 by hand, the gate's own sync_base then merged master into the branch, and `cap gate local-env --full` ran an opus Gate A and a sonnet Gate B against a diff of nothing. Both verdicts were recorded against fingerprint e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855, which is the SHA-256 of the empty string, and gate_ready compares that to a tree fingerprint that is also the empty hash, so two PASSes there would have read as ready. The review was salvaged only because Gate A noticed the empty diff itself and reviewed the landed range instead. The same blind spot is why the reminder hook still lists local-env as "done and unlanded" with nothing left to land. cap gate should refuse when the reviewable diff is empty and say the work is already in the base, and gate_ready should never treat the empty-string fingerprint as a match. Not fixed here because bin/cap-gate and bin/lib.sh are both owned by the cap-headless task right now.

text: Piping `cap verify` into anything hangs forever after the run finishes, because the checks start detached containers that inherit the pipe. `cap verify --repo classroom | tail -30` sat with a live `tail` and no writer for twelve minutes; the process tree showed `bash---tail` and nothing else, so `cap verify` had already exited. podman's conmon, php-fpm and the cron loop all keep the inherited write end of that pipe open after `compose up -d` returns, so `tail` never sees EOF and never prints the buffered output. Killing it destroyed a seven-minute run's entire output, and the run had genuinely failed (port 8080 was held by another worktree's stack), so the reason was lost with it. Redirecting to a file instead of piping avoids it completely. Worth deciding whether cap-verify should write its own log and print a summary so a caller never reaches for a pipe, or whether the devstack tasks should start containers with their fds closed. The general shape applies to any cap command that brings a container stack up, not just verify.

text: `cap gate --full` re-runs gate B even when gate.json already holds a PASS for B at the current fingerprint. Hit today on cap-headless: B passed at fingerprint c6dfe1b4 at 01:25, and the `--full` run needed only for gate A paid for a second full Sonnet review of the identical diff. The fingerprint is already the mechanism that answers this, so the loop should skip a profile whose recorded verdict matches the current fingerprint unless asked to re-review. Not fixed now because bin/cap-gate is owned by the cap-headless task, which is mid-round.

text: `cap land --merge` squashes, which destroys work the harness just asked for. rules/commits.md tells every agent that "a summary that resists one line is doing more than one logical change. Split it with `git add -p`", and cap check enforces the comment rules that go with it. devstack-ports had genuinely done two things, a per-worktree port derivation and a fix for container-written PDFs the host user could not delete, so it was sent back and split into two commits with two separate rationales. `gh pr merge --squash` would have collapsed both into one commit whose message could only describe one of them, undoing the split and the round trip that produced it. Landed with `gh pr merge --rebase` by hand instead, which is also what the two earlier classroom PRs used, so master's history is rebase-shaped and cap-land is the only thing that would have squashed. Either cap-land should take the merge strategy as a flag, or it should default to rebase and let squash be the explicit choice, but it should not silently contradict the rule the rest of the pipeline spends rounds enforcing.

text: `cap commit` writes commit messages and does not enforce the commit rules `cap land` refuses on, so a branch accumulates violations for its whole life and only finds out at the landing gate. Hit on cap-headless: 32 of 83 commits carried summary lines over the 50-character limit rules/commits.md sets, and cap land (which grew the check in 26e0a54, 2026-09-09) rejected the whole branch after both gates had already PASSed. The cost is a rewrite of 32 commits across a branch with two merge commits in it, at the one moment the branch is otherwise finished. The writer and the checker must share one implementation: cap-commit should apply the same rule at the moment it writes, where a bad summary costs one retry instead of a rebase. Note also that master's own last 20 commits contain 6 violations, so the rule is enforced on landing but was never applied retroactively, and commits that predate 26e0a54 or landed by another path are already non-compliant.

text: `cap drop` removes the worktree and leaves its container stack running. devstack-devstack-ports' four containers were still up nine hours after the task was dropped, holding a db, php-fpm, nginx and a cron loop for a checkout that no longer exists. On this box that is not untidiness: 7GB of RAM is the binding constraint on how many tasks can run at once, each stack is around a gigabyte, and clearing two sets of orphans took available memory from 3GB back to 4GB. It is also the likeliest explanation for the harness memory guard killing a backgrounded cap-gate earlier in the same session. The stack is trivially identifiable, since lib.sh derives COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME from the repository path and cap-drop knows that path, so cap-drop could bring it down before removing the worktree. Note that `mise run dev:down` cannot be relied on for this after the fact: once the worktree is gone the task file is gone with it, and the engine probe in the remaining checkout may resolve differently than it did when the stack was created.

text: The peak memory a project records is a high-water mark that never decays, so one unlucky build throttles every later wave. aula's recorded peak is 2910 MB; the seven `cap verify` runs measured since have peaked between 1839 and 2470 MB. `cap wave spawn` divides free memory by the recorded peak, so it offered one slot at a time through a three-row wave that would have fit two, and the wave took three sequential rounds instead of two. A trailing median or a decaying maximum would track the project as it actually is now.

text: `cap commit` wrote a body that restated the diff for all five commits it produced this session, and split one logical change into two commits whose halves cannot stand alone (a compose file and the document explaining it). rules/commits.md says the body must state why, not what, and `cap land` does not check bodies, only the summary line, so nothing catches it. Every message had to be rewritten by hand before landing. Related to the entry above on `cap commit` not enforcing the rules `cap land` refuses on; this is the same gap measured at 5 of 5.

text:
No command grants a path to a task's owns list

The ownership hook refuses a write outside `state/tasks/<slug>/owns`, which is
correct. When the refusal is right but the path should have been granted, the
captain has to know that the list is a plain file in the hub and append to it by
hand. There is no `cap grant <slug> <path>`, so the recovery step is the one
part of the mechanism that only works if you already know the internals.

Hit on 2026-09-11: `cap-owner` was asked to delete the `CAP_ENV_SCRUB` global,
which required editing `bin/cap-ask`. The hook blocked it, the agent reported the
block, and the fix was `printf 'bin/cap-ask\n' >> state/tasks/cap-owner/owns`.

Not fixed now because `bin/cap` and the spawn path belong to the `cap-owner`
task, which is three rounds deep on multi-captain ownership. Adding a second
ownership mechanism to that branch would widen a task that is close to landing.

Recurrence: this exact shape hit cicat-carrito three times in one afternoon
(2026-09-11). PagePlaceholder.tsx's deletion, then VolverLink.tsx, then
CourseNotFoundBanner.tsx, each a new shared-component extraction the running
task correctly refused to create via a guard-bypassing `rm`/`Write` workaround,
instead reporting the block and waiting. Widening `owns` by hand each time
cost one full round-trip per file. Worth prioritizing now that it is a
recurring tax on exactly the pattern (extract cross-cutting duplication into a
shared component mid-task) the review rounds keep asking for.

text: `cap gate`, `cap commit`, and `cap check` give the captain session no way to notice completion other than blocking on them or hand-rolling a poll loop, because they are foreground CLI commands with no herdr pane and no state-file signal the reminder hook reads. A crew pane's stop already surfaces automatically as "has stopped and is waiting on you", but a `cap gate --full` run started in the background has nothing equivalent: the captain caught a session writing its own `until kill -0 $pid` watcher twice in one sitting and said the harness should raise this, not the session. The fix is the same reminder-hook mechanism crew panes use, extended to these dispatch commands, not another watcher pattern to remember to reach for. Not fixed now: surfaced while `pipeline-hardening`, the task that owns `bin/cap-gate`/`bin/lib.sh`, was mid-review.

subject: send
text: cap send addresses a task by slug, so a gate, commit or cleanup session started by cap ask cannot be steered from the command line while it runs, only by typing into its pane (labelled gate-A-<slug> and so on). The session is real and interactive; only the addressing is missing.
